If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061989/assets/00a9df76d0be8ffd33b2ee968b57a21eb1e6947af6e94505313f163b584f5769.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(2x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-12.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 8+2\cdot (-12)=-8.
$$
html:
If F is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C. In this case, we have

∮CF⋅nds=∫C1F⋅n1ds+∫C2F⋅n2ds+∫C3F⋅n3ds+∫C4F⋅n4ds,

where the sides Ci and unit vectors ni are shown below.

We compute this integral in two stages.

  • First, consider the side C1. We have that n1=i, and therefore, ∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C1(2xi−3yj)⋅ids=2∫C1xds. This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side C1, we have r(t)=2i+tj,⇒r′(t)=j,t∈[−1,1]. Therefore, 2∫C1xds=2∫−112⋅||r′(t)||dt=4∫−11dt=4⋅2=8. By symmetry, the flux integral across the side C3 must be the same. Therefore, ∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C3F⋅n3ds=8.
  • Next, we consider the side C2. We have that n2=j, and therefore, ∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2(2xi−3yj)⋅jds=−3∫C2yds. This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side C2, we have r(t)=ti+j,⇒r′(t)=i,t∈[−2,2]. Therefore, −3∫C2yds=−3∫−221⋅||r′(t)||dt=−3∫−22dt=(−3)⋅4=−12. By symmetry, the flux integral across the side C4 must be the same. Therefore, ∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C4F⋅n4ds=−12.

Finally, then

∮CF⋅nds=2⋅8+2⋅(−12)=−8.
